Matt Brown explained that Fellow could be deployed company-wide through Okta, with all users treated as billable, or rolled out in stages by importing a CSV of selected paid users while allowing other teams access to Fellow. For a staged rollout, Fellow could use quarterly true-ups; for example, a deployment might begin with 500 users and increase to 750 the following quarter.

Nick Sarkesian asked whether a quarterly true-up would allow the customer to add enterprise licenses mid-quarter and be billed for the period those additional users were active. Matt Brown said the plan would be flat-rate, allowing users to be added without contacting an account manager or support; at the end of the billing period, Fellow would review active users and adjust billing. Matt said access could not be split among different plan tiers: the plan would be all-or-nothing.

Trina Berks asked whether the license count could be reduced if users stopped using Fellow. Matt Brown said Fellow could distinguish active users from people who had merely signed in once, and that billing would not count everyone who received access through Okta if only a smaller group was actively using the product. Matt encouraged starting with users already committed to using Fellow and said Fellow had resources to help build adoption.

Matt Brown agreed to send Eric Cameron and the customer team security and compliance documentation, information about Fellow’s Okta integration, SOC 2 and MPA documentation for DocuSign signature, information about the Jira integration, and an overview of Fellow’s onboarding methodology. Matt described a 30-day onboarding methodology for getting users on paid licenses up and running after an enterprise rollout is committed to.

Eric Cameron said the customer would activate Pro licenses for the team members currently testing Fellow, but would not make an enterprise-level decision until Nick Sarkesian and the team had reviewed the documentation from Matt Brown. Eric said the customer probably would not begin a full enterprise rollout until the beginning of 2024.

Matt Brown said 20 users had been active during the previous month and proposed switching those users to Fellow’s annual Pro rate. He said additional users could either be invited by existing paid users or restricted to invitations from designated administrators, depending on the workspace configuration.

Eric Cameron and Nick Sarkesian agreed that workspace invitations could be managed by both of them, so either could add users. Matt Brown recommended keeping invitations open in the short term to encourage organic adoption, then estimating the size of the first enterprise deployment stage after a month or two.

Eric Cameron asked Matt Brown to remove Tyler and Alex as Fellow administrators and make Eric Cameron, Nick Sarkesian, and Trina Berks administrators instead. Matt agreed, noted that Alex had already agreed to be removed, and promised to confirm by email after completing the changes.

The requested behavior was to check queued notifications, mark existing queue entries as queued, upsert notifications not yet in the queue, set new notifications’ `timestamp` and `queued=True`, and deactivate active notifications from the same source that are absent from the current notification IDs.

On 2023-05-25, after the user asked to add the proposed improvements, the assistant provided a `NotificationHandler` implementation with `modify_request` and `get_request_update` as class methods, type hints, a `log_upsert_results` placeholder whose body is `pass`, and exception handling around `bulk_write`. The implementation builds `UpdateOne` operations for existing records with `queued=False`, builds upserts keyed by `notification_id`, applies a bulk write if operations exist, updates records with null `timestamp` and `queued` to timestamped and queued, then deactivates active records of the given `source` whose IDs are not in the current set. The assistant said the changes improved modularity and maintainability.

The assistant’s revised notification code mutates each input request in `modify_request` by adding `notification_id` and `source`, then removing `_id`; `log_upsert_results` is not actually implemented. It also retains the legacy collection `.update(..., multi=True)` calls and performs separate update and upsert operations for each input notification.

records.text: On 2023-05-29, the user asked for an explanation of the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) concept of “effective control” in the voice of a RAND military researcher. The assistant described it as the ability to assert dominance and maintain control in a specific area, especially a contested region, through military, economic, political, and diplomatic efforts—not merely physical troop presence, but also influence over other actors.

On 2023-05-29, the assistant identified five elements of the PLA’s “effective control” approach: military presence and capability to deter adversaries; intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) for domain awareness; political and diplomatic influence over regional actors; economic leverage through aid or investment; and rapid crisis response combined with escalation control through force, negotiation, or diplomacy. The assistant said the approach aims to secure China’s territorial claims, deter potential adversaries, and maintain regional stability.

On 2023-05-29, the user asked how “intelligentized” and “informatized” warfare connect to and enable PLA “effective control.” The assistant characterized informatized warfare as integrating information and communications technology into military operations, including collecting, analyzing, disseminating, and exploiting information using tools such as satellite communications, computer networks, and electronic warfare.

On 2023-05-29, the assistant said informatized warfare could support PLA effective control by improving command and control, ISR, domain awareness, decision-making, and response speed, and by enabling more efficient use of military resources.

On 2023-05-29, the assistant described intelligentized warfare as extending informatized warfare through artificial intelligence, machine learning, autonomous systems, advanced data analysis, and decision-making algorithms. It said these technologies could speed and improve decisions, resource allocation, ISR, situational awareness, crisis response, and escalation control, thereby helping the PLA pursue effective control in contested regions.
